We will then cover the checks at intersections, in your rearview mirror and over your shoulder, and why keeping track of traffic in every direction helps you make quick and safe decisions on the road. In short: Look left and right at intersections; check the rearview mirror often; spot tailgaters early.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s3","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Scanning is not following","fact_ids":["sec06-R03","sec06-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Block ahead: how far to look.","fact_ids":["sec06-R03","sec06-F01"]},{"text":"Seconds count: how far to follow.","fact_ids":["sec06-R03","sec06-F01"]},{"text":"Two separate rules.","fact_ids":["sec06-R03","sec06-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a mix-up to avoid. The block-ahead rule and the following-distance rule both deal with what is in front of you, so people blend them. Looking about one city block ahead is the scanning rule, and it is separate from the seconds-based count used for following distance. Keep each in its place: your eyes reach about a block down the road, while your car stays a counted number of seconds behind the vehicle ahead. Two rules, two jobs. In short: Block ahead: how far to look; seconds count: how far to follow; two separate rules.","fact_ids":["sec06-R03","sec06-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Before you change lanes","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Check the side mirrors.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-F05"]},{"text":"Turn your head over your shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-F05"]},{"text":"Track traffic on every side.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Lane changes need their own checks. Before a lane change, check the side mirrors and also turn your head to look over your shoulder. And the reason for all this looking is simple. When you keep track of how fast and where the traffic is in front, behind and on both sides, you can make decisions quickly and safely. The shoulder check covers what the side mirrors may not show, and keeping track of every side ties the two habits together into one quick, safe decision. In short: Check the side mirrors; turn your head over your shoulder; track traffic on every side.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the lane change","fact_ids":["sec06-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"About to change lanes.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04"]},{"text":"Which two checks?","fact_ids":["sec06-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are about to change lanes. Before a lane change, check the side mirrors and also turn your head to look over your shoulder. Mirrors by themselves leave gaps beside you, which is why the shoulder check is part of the routine every time you move over. Both checks belong to the same routine, and both come before you begin to move over into the next lane. In short: A block ahead; left and right; mirrors often; shoulder check before changing lanes.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03","sec06-F04","sec06-F05","sec06-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec06-u02","module_id":"sec06-m02","objective_ids":["sec06-u02"],"title":{"text":"Following distance","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-F07","sec06-R01"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Following too closely causes most rear-end crashes, so the right gap is one of the most useful habits you can build.","fact_ids":["sec06-F13","sec06-F06"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Sara follows a truck on a dry road and picks a sign as her fixed point.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06"]},"reasoning":{"text":"When the truck passes the sign she counts from one-thousand-one and reaches the sign at one-thousand-two.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-F07"]},"result":{"text":"She finished the count too early, so she is following too closely and drops back.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-F13"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking the four-second example is the cushion the manual sets for poor conditions.","fact_ids":["sec06-R01"]},"correction":{"text":"The example count to four takes about four seconds, while poor conditions call for a cushion of three to six seconds.","fact_ids":["sec06-R01","sec06-F07","sec06-F09"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Count it out; add more when speed or weather worsens.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"The road is wet and slick. Each of these ideas builds on the one before, from measuring the gap to adjusting it for speed and weather. That is why the manual ties following distance to speed: the faster you go, the more room you leave in front of you. Here is the idea. Space around your vehicle gives you and other drivers time to react to emergencies, and staying in the middle of your lane helps create that cushion. Keep enough room ahead of you to stop suddenly, and enough room ahead and behind to pass or stop safely. In the slides ahead we look at bicycles in your lane, how to help the driver behind you, and what to do when someone follows you too closely. In short: Space gives time to react; stay in the middle of your lane; room ahead and behind.","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Bicycles in your lane","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"At least three feet.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-R02"]},{"text":"Moderate your speed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-R02"]},{"text":"Feet beside, not seconds behind.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Bicycles get a specific rule. Following distance is counted in seconds behind the vehicle ahead, while bicycle clearance in a shared lane is a fixed three feet to the side. So for a bicycle, think of a gap of at least three feet to the side, while for the car ahead, think of a gap counted in seconds. In short: At least three feet; moderate your speed; feet beside, not seconds behind.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Helping the driver behind","fact_ids":["sec06-F15","sec06-F18"]},"lines":[{"text":"Hold a steady speed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F15","sec06-F18"]},{"text":"Signal early before slowing.","fact_ids":["sec06-F15","sec06-F18"]},{"text":"Sudden stops affect others.","fact_ids":["sec06-F15","sec06-F18"]}],"narration":{"text":"You can protect yourself by helping the car behind you. What you do affects the driver behind you, especially when you have to stop suddenly. A steady speed and an early signal give that driver the time they need. Both habits give the driver behind you time to react to what you do next. Steady and early is the pattern. In short: Hold a steady speed; signal early before slowing; sudden stops affect others.","fact_ids":["sec06-F15","sec06-F18"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Do not brake to scold","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Slow gradually.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"Open more space ahead.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"Brake gently when you must.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. If someone is tailgating you, slow down gradually and open more space ahead, so you can brake more gently and give the tailgater time to react. A tailgater is handled by slowing gradually and adding space ahead of you, which lets you brake more gently when you must stop. The extra space ahead is your protection, because it means you will not have to stop hard with someone right behind you. In short: Slow gradually; open more space ahead; brake gently when you must.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Letting a tailgater by","fact_ids":["sec06-F17","sec06-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Change lanes when it is safe.","fact_ids":["sec06-F17","sec06-F04"]},{"text":"Let the tailgater go around.","fact_ids":["sec06-F17","sec06-F04"]},{"text":"Keep your cushion.","fact_ids":["sec06-F17","sec06-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"There is a second way to handle a tailgater. Once the other driver has gone around, you have your space cushion back on every side. Changing lanes and slowing gradually are the two responses the manual gives, and both aim at the same result: more space between you and a driver who is too close. In short: Change lanes when it is safe; let the tailgater go around; keep your cushion.","fact_ids":["sec06-F17","sec06-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the tailgater rule","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R04","sec06-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"A driver is right behind you.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R04","sec06-F17"]},{"text":"What should you do?","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R04","sec06-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a driver is following you far too closely.
